summary.text: A quadratic equation contains only non-negative whole-number powers of x, so it is a second-degree polynomial equation.
With real coefficients it has zero, one or two distinct real roots, and always two roots when complex ones count and a double root counts twice.
It can be solved by factoring, by completing the square or by a formula in a, b and c, and such problems were known as early as 2000 BC.

items.explain: A quadratic equation with arbitrary complex coefficients always has two complex-valued roots, which may or may not be distinct.

steps.text: To solve x² + 5x + 6 = 0, look for two numbers that add to 5 and multiply to 6.
Those numbers are 2 and 3, so it factors as (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0.
A product is zero only if one factor is zero, so x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0.
So the solutions are x = 2 and x = 3.

paragraphs.heading: A second-degree equation
paragraphs.text: A quadratic equation is one in which x appears only with powers that are whole numbers of zero or more, which makes it a polynomial equation. Its highest power is two, so it is a polynomial equation of the second degree. The values of x that make it true are its solutions, also called the roots or zeros of the quadratic function on the left side. There are never more than two.

paragraphs.heading: How many roots
paragraphs.text: When the coefficients are real numbers, a quadratic equation has zero, one or two distinct real roots. A single root can be seen as two roots sharing one value, and is then called a double root. When there are no real roots, the equation still has two complex roots, and they are complex conjugates of each other. So once complex roots are allowed and a double root is counted twice, there are always exactly two roots.

paragraphs.heading: Factoring by inspection
paragraphs.text: For most students, the first method learned is factoring by inspection. The aim is to turn ax² + bx + c = 0 into the form (px + q)(rx + s) = 0, sometimes just by spotting suitable numbers. By the Zero Factor Property, the equation then holds if px + q = 0 or rx + s = 0, and solving those two linear equations gives the roots. For x² + bx + c = 0, you hunt for two numbers whose sum is b and whose product is c. For example, x² + 5x + 6 can be written as (x + 3)(x + 2).

paragraphs.heading: Where factoring fails
paragraphs.text: When a is not 1, finding the factors can take a lot of guessing and checking, if it can be done by inspection at all. Apart from special cases such as b = 0 or c = 0, the method only works when the roots are rational. As a result, most quadratic equations that come up in practice cannot be solved this way.

paragraphs.heading: Completing the square
paragraphs.text: Another method is completing the square. Take b/a, the coefficient of x, halve it, square it, and add the result to both sides, which turns the left side into a perfect square. You then write the left side as a square and set its square root equal to the positive and to the negative square root of the right side. That gives two linear equations, and the ± sign records both answers, as in x = −1 + √3 and x = −1 − √3.

paragraphs.heading: The quadratic formula
paragraphs.text: Applied to the general equation, completing the square yields the quadratic formula. Expanding shows the equation is equivalent to (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac)/4a². Then square-rooting each side and getting x on its own gives x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a, which states the solutions directly in terms of a, b and c. Problems that can be put as quadratic equations were being solved as early as 2000 BC.

paragraphs.heading: A lesser-known version
paragraphs.text: Muller's method uses another form of the formula, x = 2c/(−b ± √(b² − 4ac)). It can be reached from the usual one through Vieta's formulas, which say the product of the roots is c/a. Its strength shows when a = 0: the equation becomes linear with one root, and this form still gives that root. The usual formula, in that case, runs into division by zero for one root and the indeterminate form 0/0 for the other.
